> Bioinformatics is what happens when a biological question produces more data
> than a person can look at.

## Learning objectives

1. Describe the path from biological sample to analysable data.
2. Name the major sequencing data formats and what each one holds.
3. Explain why file size and file *shape* are different problems.
4. Recognise that every dataset carries the fingerprints of how it was made.

## A working definition

Bioinformatics is the use of computation to answer biological questions. That
is deliberately broad, because the field is broad. In practice it usually means
one of three things:

- **Processing** — turning raw instrument output into something interpretable
  (reads → aligned sequences → variants).
- **Analysis** — asking a question of the processed data (is this variant
  associated with disease?).
- **Interpretation** — deciding what the answer means biologically, and whether
  to believe it.

Most training focuses on the middle step. Most mistakes happen in the first and
last.

## Where the data comes from

Every dataset in this workshop began as material from a person, a virus, or a
culture. The chain looks like this:

```
sample → extraction → library prep → sequencing → basecalling → reads
```

Each arrow loses something and adds something. Extraction favours some
templates over others. Library prep introduces PCR duplicates and adapter
sequence. Basecalling makes probabilistic guesses at each position.

::: {.callout-important}
## The central point of this whole section
By the time data reaches your laptop, it has been transformed five times.
Artifacts from any of those steps are indistinguishable from biology **unless
you know the steps happened.**
:::

## The formats you will meet

| Format | Holds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **FASTA** | Sequences + names | No quality information. Deceptively simple. |
| **FASTQ** | Sequences + per-base quality | The raw output of most sequencers. |
| **SAM/BAM** | Reads aligned to a reference | BAM is compressed SAM. Needs an index. |
| **VCF** | Variants relative to a reference | Positions are 1-based. Meaningless without knowing the reference. |
| **Newick** | Tree topology + branch lengths | A tree in a line of text. |

A FASTA record:

```
>hbv_R02B35_consensus
GCTGCTATGCCTCATCTTCTTGTTGGTTCTTCTGGACTATCAAGGTATGTTGCCCGTTTG
```

A FASTQ record for the same read — same sequence, plus what the machine thought
of each base:

```
@hbv_R02B35_read1
GCTGCTATGCCTCATCTTCTTGTTGGTTCTTCTGGACTATCAAGGTATGT
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIHHHHHGGGGFFFEEDDCCBA@?>=<;:98
```

That fourth line is the part beginners discard and regret. Each character
encodes a Phred score: the machine's estimate of the probability this base is
wrong.

::: {.callout-note}
## Phred scores in one line
Q30 means a 1-in-1,000 chance the base is wrong. Q20 is 1-in-100. Q10 is
1-in-10. The scale is logarithmic, so the difference between Q30 and Q20 is
much larger than it looks.
:::

## Why "big data" is the wrong frame

Sequencing data is large, but size is the least interesting problem. The hard
parts are:

- **Shape** — data arrives with samples in columns and features in rows, or the
  reverse, and nothing tells you which.
- **Missingness** — a blank cell might mean "not measured", "measured as zero",
  or "measured and failed QC". These demand different handling.
- **Provenance** — the same sample sequenced twice on different runs will not
  produce identical results.

You will meet all three in the [hands-on case study](../4-hands-on/index.qmd),
where a dataset that looks clean turns out to have a fatal design problem that
no amount of computation can fix.

## Check yourself

1. You are given a FASTA file and asked to assess sequencing quality. What do
   you tell the person who asked?
2. A collaborator sends a VCF with no reference genome specified. What can you
   conclude from it?
3. Why might the same sample yield different variant calls on two runs?

Answers are discussed in the [exercise](exercise.qmd).
